Digestive.label: Vomiting
Digestive.desc: Frequent throwing up food, bile, or foam

Digestive.label: Bloody Stool (Hematochezia/Melena)
Digestive.desc: Dark tarry or bright red blood in feces

Digestive.label: Anorexia / Loss of Appetite
Digestive.desc: Refusal to eat food or drink water

Skin & Coat.label: Intense Scratching / Pruritus
Skin & Coat.desc: Persistent scratching, licking, or biting skin

Skin & Coat.label: Scabs & Crusts
Skin & Coat.desc: Dry flaking, crusty lesions or sores

Skin & Coat.label: Pustules / Papules / Rash
Skin & Coat.desc: Small pimples, hot spots, or raised bumps

Skin & Coat.label: Foul Odor from Skin / Coat
Skin & Coat.desc: Yeasty, rancid, or sour smell from pet

Skin & Coat.label: Ear Discharge / Waxy Buildup
Skin & Coat.desc: Dark brown or yellow discharge in ear canal

Skin & Coat.label: Head Shaking / Tilting
Skin & Coat.desc: Vigorous or repetitive shaking of ears and head

Respiratory.label: Nasal Discharge
Respiratory.desc: Clear, mucoid, or yellowish discharge from nostrils

Respiratory.label: Coughing / Hacking
Respiratory.desc: Dry goose-honk or moist productive cough

Respiratory.label: Eye Discharge (Ocular Secretions)
Respiratory.desc: Crusty, watery, or purulent drainage around eyes

Respiratory.label: Labored Breathing / Wheezing
Respiratory.desc: Open-mouth breathing, flared nostrils, shortness of breath

Behavioral & Systemic.label: Fever / Hyperthermia
Behavioral & Systemic.desc: Body feels abnormally warm, lethargy with chills

Behavioral & Systemic.label: Extreme Lethargy / Depression
Behavioral & Systemic.desc: Severe unresponsiveness, lack of energy to walk

Behavioral & Systemic.label: Pale or White Gums / Mucosa
Behavioral & Systemic.desc: Loss of healthy pink gum coloration (anemia sign)

Behavioral & Systemic.label: Stiffness / Reluctance to Move
Behavioral & Systemic.desc: Joint stiffness, hesitance to climb stairs or stand

Canine Parvovirus.summary: Severe, highly contagious viral illness predominantly affecting puppies and unvaccinated dogs.
Canine Parvovirus.why_matches: Marked by acute bloody diarrhea, persistent vomiting, severe dehydration, and extreme lethargy, particularly dangerous in young canines.
recommended_steps: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency veterinary intensive care within hours.
Do NOT attempt home treatment; intravenous fluid therapy and antiemetics are lifesaving.
Isolate the pet completely from all other dogs; parvo spreads rapidly via footwear and surfaces.
Disinfect living quarters with diluted bleach solution (1:32 ratio).

Feline Upper Respiratory Infection.summary: Common feline complex (Cat Flu) caused by Feline Herpesvirus-1 (FHV-1) or Calicivirus.
Feline Upper Respiratory Infection.why_matches: Pronounced sneezing, bilateral nasal and ocular discharge, conjunctivitis, and moderate fever in felines.
recommended_steps: Schedule a veterinary evaluation within 24–48 hours for antibiotics/antivirals if discharge is mucopurulent.
Gently wipe crusts from nostrils and eyelids with a warm, damp cotton ball.
Place pet in a steamy bathroom for 10-15 minutes twice daily to loosen congestion.
Warm strongly-scented canned food to stimulate appetite through olfactory impairment.

Allergic Dermatitis.summary: Hypersensitivity immune response driven by environmental atopy, food proteins, or contact allergens.
Allergic Dermatitis.why_matches: Severe, chronic pruritus (scratching), ventral erythema, secondary excoriations, and patchy hair thinning.
recommended_steps: Schedule a clinical veterinary consult for cytological evaluation and targeted antipruritic therapy (e.g., Apoquel, Cytopoint).
Fit an Elizabethan collar (cone) to break the itch-scratch-trauma cycle.
Bathe in cool water using veterinarian-approved colloidal oatmeal or chlorhexidine shampoo.
Review dietary ingredients with your veterinarian to formulate an elimination trial.

Otitis Externa.summary: Acute or chronic inflammation and secondary infection (Malassezia yeast or bacteria) of the external ear canal.
Otitis Externa.why_matches: Vigorous head shaking, dark malodorous waxy exudate, localized ear pinna scratching, and vocalized discomfort upon touching the ears.
recommended_steps: Have your vet perform ear cytology to identify the precise causative organism (yeast vs rod/cocci bacteria).
Do NOT insert Q-tips or cotton swabs into the ear canal, as this risks rupturing the tympanic membrane.
Administer vet-prescribed topical otic drops consistently for the full prescribed duration.
Dry ears thoroughly after baths or swimming sessions.

Acute Gastroenteritis.summary: Sudden gastrointestinal inflammation frequently triggered by dietary indiscretion, spoiled food, or minor pathogens.
Acute Gastroenteritis.why_matches: Sudden onset of vomiting and watery diarrhea without profound systemic organ failure, accompanied by abdominal discomfort.
recommended_steps: Withhold solid food for 8–12 hours (only for adult animals; NEVER fast puppies, kittens, or diabetic pets).
Offer small sips of clean water or oral electrolyte solution every 30 minutes to gauge retention.
Transition gradually to a bland diet (boiled chicken breast and plain white rice in a 1:2 ratio) for 3–5 days.
Contact a veterinarian promptly if vomiting persists beyond 24 hours or blood appears in vomit.

Canine Tick Fever.summary: Vector-borne systemic infection (Ehrlichiosis / Babesiosis / Anaplasmosis) transmitted by Rhipicephalus tick bites.
Canine Tick Fever.why_matches: High spiking fever, striking pale/anemic oral mucosa, profound lethargy, joint reluctance to move, and thrombocytopenia risk.
recommended_steps: Transport pet to a veterinary hospital immediately for a Complete Blood Count (CBC) and tick-borne pathogen PCR/SNAP test.
Prompt administration of doxycycline or specific antiprotozoal injections can be curative if initiated early.
Monitor gums for petechiae (pinpoint red spots) or nosebleeds indicative of low platelet count.
Initiate strict veterinary tick prevention treatments (isoxazoline oral chews or collars).

Ringworm (Dermatophytosis).summary: Zoonotic fungal skin infection caused by Microsporum canis or Trichophyton mentagrophytes.
Ringworm (Dermatophytosis).why_matches: Well-demarcated circular alopecia (bald spots), silvery scales, crusting, and mild inflammatory perimeter with minimal severe pruritus.
recommended_steps: Consult a veterinarian for Wood's lamp examination and fungal culture confirmation.
WEAR GLOVES when touching lesions; Ringworm is highly zoonotic and readily spreads to humans and children.
Apply vet-prescribed topical antifungal miconazole/ketoconazole creams and oral antifungals if widespread.
Wash all pet bedding, rugs, and grooming brushes in hot bleach-diluted water.

Sarcoptic / Demodectic Mange.summary: Parasitic mite infestation (Sarcoptes scabiei burrowing mites or Demodex follicular mites).
Sarcoptic / Demodectic Mange.why_matches: Relentless, frenzied scratching, extensive crusted thickening on ear margins, elbows, and hocks, accompanied by musty sebum odor.
recommended_steps: Visit the vet for deep skin scrapes to microscopic visualize mite species.
Administer modern isoxazoline parasiticides (e.g., Sarolaner, Fluralaner) as prescribed.
Isolate the pet from other household animals until two negative skin scrapings are achieved.
Wash household textiles on maximum heat setting.

Flea Allergy Dermatitis.summary: Hypersensitivity reaction triggered by antigens present in flea salivary proteins.
Flea Allergy Dermatitis.why_matches: Severe biting at lumbar spine, base of tail, inner thighs, showing 'flea dirt' and pinpoint scabbed crusts.
recommended_steps: Use a fine-toothed metal flea comb over wet paper towels to reveal telltale reddish-black flea dirt.
Apply an EPA/FDA-approved veterinary fast-kill adulticide (e.g., nitenpyram) and preventative monthly topical/oral protection.
Vacuum carpets, baseboards, and couch cushions daily, discarding the vacuum bag outdoors.
Treat ALL dogs and cats in the residence simultaneously.

Infectious Conjunctivitis.summary: Inflammation of the conjunctival mucosal membranes caused by bacterial, viral, or foreign body irritants.
Infectious Conjunctivitis.why_matches: Mucopurulent ocular secretions, eyelid squinting (blepharospasm), hyperemic red conjunctiva, and pawing at eyes.
recommended_steps: Have a vet conduct a fluorescein corneal stain to rule out corneal ulcers before applying any steroid-containing drops.
Flush discharge gently with sterile saline eye wash.
Do NOT use human eye drops or leftover medications.
Fit a protective collar if the pet rubs eyes against rugs or with paws.
